items.title: Winners and losers from Spanish GP F1 qualifying at the Madring
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Just 0.011s separate first and second in the first-ever Formula 1 qualifying session at the Madring, and the first four slots on the Spanish Grand Prix grid will be occupied by drivers from four different teams too.

But considering all the fears of a Sunday procession, is this the end of the action?

And if it is, who's maximised their opportunity, and who's been found wanting?

Loser: Oscar Piastri (7th)

Eighth in Q1, ninth in Q2...Piastri was well off the pace throughout qualifying.

He had to abort his first flying lap of Q1 and, from then on, it was a "messy" session by his reckoning.

He even called it a "pretty crap" go in Q3, as he laboured to seventh.

"That's how it goes sometimes unfortunately," he said. "It's been a bit of a better weekend, like Monza, in that I at least am...happier with what the car's doing, and today was simply just one of those sessions."

More painful will be the fact that it's expected to be hard to overtake here. And even more painful will be the fact that team-mate Lando Norris took a stunning pole position - so the pace was definitely there.

Piastri's middling run continues.

Winner: Lando Norris (1st)

A winner not just because of the end result, but because of the manner in which it arrived - pretty much out of nowhere.

The earlier stages of qualifying suggested this would be a fight between Mercedes and Ferrari, with Max Verstappen's Red Bull maybe interloping.

Norris was fifth in Q1 but only seventh in Q2, and when Kimi Antonelli stuck his Mercedes on provisional pole with the first 1m31s lap of the weekend, having been narrowly usurped by Lewis Hamilton in the first Q3 runs, it looked at though the session was going to form.

But then came Norris, with a full-send, ultra-committed lap in his McLaren.

The last corner was untidy - team principal Andrea Stella reckoned Norris lost three tenths there - but the rest of it Stella called "a masterpiece", and what Norris reckoned was probably the best qualifying lap of his entire career was enough to snatch pole from Antonelli by a hundredth of a second.

Not totally clean from the world champion, but certainly brilliant.

Loser: George Russell (6th)

Gap to Antonelli in pace: 0.314s (not great)Gap to Antonelli in positions: four (also not great)

Russell seemed shake off his brush with the wall in Q1, a session he ended up topping, pretty easily and said he felt in a good place afterwards - claiming he was "about three tenths up" on his previous best midway round his final Q3 lap.

"Tried pushing hard in Turn 11, the tyres couldn't take it and then lost all the laptime thereafter," said Russell, who added it has been "really challenging" to judge how hard to lean on the tyres.

Salvaging a time loss in that three-tenth ballpark obviously would've made a difference to his grid position. But after a promising start to the weekend, qualifying was another example of Russell being a step behind at Mercedes - and barely being able to grasp at any title hopes right now.

Winner: Lewis Hamilton (4th)

Hamilton outqualified Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc by just 0.006s and did well to take a place on the second row after crashing and losing time in FP3.

The seven-time champion delivered a terse post-qualifying summary as he recalled a "pretty straightforward" session and praised "good execution" from the team.

"I'm going to have fun, that's all I can say, I’m going to have real fun, I'm not going to put too much pressure on it," he said.

Leclerc, who is using an older-spec Ferrari engine after his Monza crash, said he lost time through sector one in particular.

"I think most of the people put a new power unit or a newer-spec [in for qualifying], and I kind of had the same spec - and that's on me obviously for last week - so maybe I didn't do the step forward that the others did on that side," he said.

"But having said that I think the lap was quite clean. I've had a few moments here and there, which I maybe lost a little bit and when I see how close it is, it's frustrating but at the same time I feel like if you ask any drivers on the grid today, everybody probably can find something on the lap."

After their clash at the start of the Italian GP, the spotlight will again be on the Ferrari drivers at the start of this race in Madrid.

Loser: Ollie Bearman (21st)

That crash ruled him out of qualifying and put him a provisional 21st on the grid.

Painful - as Haas team-mate Esteban Ocon was up in 13th.

"It's a shame to be standing here right now," said Bearman as he stood watching on from the sidelines in qualifying. "The car was quick. Yesterday was a tough day but we made some changes overnight and the car was feeling really good in FP3.

"Unfortunately I got caught out in Turn 10 on that final lap."

He said worn tyres and a gust of wind contributed to his mistake.

Sunday could be Bearman's ninth-straight grand prix without points, and Haas's eighth, as Audi continues to chip away at its advantage in the fight for seventh in the constructors' championship.

Winner: Max Verstappen (3rd)

Another typical Red Bull turnaround from Friday, when technical director Pierre Wache indicated his team needed to work on set-up, mechanical grip, ride quality and energy deployment in order to get Verstappen into a better position.

The four-time champion was knocking on the door in FP3, just under four tenths off the pace, and come qualifying he was right in the mix: 0.170s off the pace in Q1 (where team-mate Liam Lawson lapped within a tenth of Russell's Mercedes) then fastest of all in Q2.

Verstappen was one of only three drivers to lap below 1m32s in Q3, enough to place him third on the grid and ahead of both Ferraris, a Mercedes and a McLaren, while Lawson faded to eighth.

Verstappen credited the car for finally doing what he wanted it to in the corners, but it's hard to escape the feeling there was also a bit of Max magic in play to make the difference in the end.

Loser: Pierre Gasly (14th)

Baffled and bemused. That's how best to describe Gasly at the end of qualifying.

"Something doesn't add up," he lamented after qualifying 14th, an uncharacteristic seven tenths off Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto in Q2.

He suggested he'd never felt such a switch from where the car had been - on Friday, it had left him confident of making the top 10 - to where it ended up.

"All my traction, I'm laying rubber every corner, sideways in all the high speed," said Gasly, who tentatively concurred when The Race asked whether this might be a deeper, set-up related issue.

Asked if he expected chaos or a procession in tomorrow's race, Gasly was in no mind to look ahead.

"At the moment I just want to get back in the office and get the answers I need."

Winner: Franco Colapinto (9th)

One place worse off on the grid compared to last weekend, as Colapinto noted, but there were plenty of reasons to be happier with this performance than Q3 at Monza.

Having gathered up a lairy moment at La Monumental on his first Q2 effort, Colapinto strung together a lap he called "amazing" that he was rightly proud of to progress to Q3.

He felt this was a track more likely to be suited to Alpine's current midfield rivals Audi and Racing Bulls, an assessment that seems to have been supported by the general trend of the weekend so far - so the Alpine had little right leading the midfield, really.

That it did owed everything to Colapinto replicating (actually improving) the laptime in Q3 - a potentially significant result on a weekend where the usually dependable Gasly has looked slightly off-colour.

Loser: Aston Martin (18th & 21st)

The Madring might be a temporary, street-style circuit, but it's still plenty fast enough and demanding enough on the power units to expose Honda.

Fernando Alonso had a mighty good go at escaping Q1, but he needed another 81 thousandths of a second to leapfrog the two Williamses - cars Aston Martin has recently been spooking with its impressive rate of chassis improvement.

Alonso felt he was losing "probably more than one second" because of the Honda engine.

At least he managed to participate in the session, though, unlike team-mate Lance Stroll, who was parked by problems with his fresh engine's water pressure.

Cadillac might be firmly in the rear view mirror now, but there's still clearly a massively long road to travel for Aston Martin to become even remotely as competitive as it wants to be and should be.

items.title: F1 2026 Spanish GP starting grid after two penalties
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Lando Norris claimed pole position for the first Spanish Grand Prix to be held on Formula 1's new Madring circuit in Madrid, ahead of F1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli.

Antonelli won't need to blast from the back to the front like he did last time out at Monza, though that may be difficult anyway given the nature of this new temporary circuit and how hard it looks to overtake on.

Most drivers behaved themselves and there were no red flags in qualifying, despite fears this track would lead to frequent crashes.

But there were a couple of grid penalties to account for: Carlos Sainz drops three places for impeding Valtteri Bottas in Q1, while Lance Stroll has a 40-place (!) penalty for taking a completely new Honda power unit that promptly sprung a water leak before he could set a time.

items.title: Winners and losers from MotoGP’s Misano sprint
items.author: Eden Hannigan
items.content:
Marc Marquez ran riot in the Misano MotoGP sprint - and he was the only rider who could really be particularly elated with how his San Marino Grand Prix Saturday has panned out.

Here are our winners and losers from the 13-lap dress rehearsal race.

Winner: Marc Marquez (1st)

Marquez had looked all through the weekend as the only rider with a real shot of stopping Bezzecchi - but it was still a surprise in the end, both that he succeeded and how easy he made it look.

After the sprint, he said that he thought a P2-P3 finish was on the cards with the soft rear. But with the medium, which he chose, "I was able to finish second-third... or victory!"

The difference-maker was the extra margin the medium granted him, seemingly in terms of the rear pushing the front, and he exploited it very well - blasting past Bezzecchi at the start and then breaking his counter-charge with a lap 11 1m30.7s scorcher. As long as Sunday's result is any kind of decent points haul, this weekend is a success.

Loser: Fabio Quartararo (21st)

Before going in too hard on Quartararo, it is important to point out - he is the only Yamaha rider who looks like doing anything of note this weekend, and he is clearly trying.

A crash is a crash, and it looked very clumsy, Quartararo trying to outfox Moreira but getting caught out under braking by what he described as "zero" rear support and running out of margin. But also a bit of a chapeau. There were a total of 11 sub-1m32s laps by Yamaha riders in this race - 10 of those were Quartararo after the crash, and the other one was Quartararo before the crash. The pace is there.

Loser: Pecco Bagnaia (13th)

“Honestly [it’s] difficult to speak about feeling when I don’t have any” was how Bagnaia opened his post-race debrief. We didn’t need him to tell us that though - the lack of feeling and control meant it was yet another fruitless sprint for the Ducati rider. 

Given Misano is a track Bagnaia has done countless laps around in the past, he could have been forgiven for expecting a slightly different outcome from this weekend. Instead, it looks to be more of the same as he’s running out of things to try to escape his troubles aboard the GP26. 

“Really frustrated but also humiliated” was how Bagnaia summed up how his struggles have made him feel. A performance like this in front of a home crowd can’t have helped his overall confidence.

Winner: Jorge Martin (3rd)

Martin lost points to both of his main title rivals at the conclusion of the 13 laps - but it looked on Friday like he would be losing a lot more than this, which is effectively bare minimum.

He was very close to an unwanted Q1 ticket yesterday, but corrected some things on the bike and in his riding - though remained outmatched in qualifying trim.

"I cannot ride with the soft [rear]," Martin lamented. "That's why I am suffering in time attack. I feel it's pushing [the front] and everything gets so aggressive, and really difficult to manage the bike."

Hence the choice of the medium for the sprint - and it clearly worked, enabling him to pick off Fermin Aldeguer and Fabio Di Giannantonio en route to a comfortable podium, even if the front was "cooked" by the laps behind the latter.

Loser: Franco Morbidelli (12th)

A rare opportunity for a genuinely good weekend in what has been a profoundly forlorn season is being squandered here for Morbidelli, who does genuinely look pretty decent on pure pace.

But with a needless long lap penalty for impeding - imagine a long sigh in the middle of this sentence - meaning his Sunday is already compromised by default, perhaps the sprint was the big chance. Instead, he looked a bit timid over the first few corners, so got roughed up by Diogo Moreira and spent the rest of the race looking for a way back - which he never did find.

Loser: Raul Fernandez/Trackhouse (7th)

If Fernandez's assessment is accurate, this is much more of a Trackhouse entry than a Fernandez entry - as he says his Q2 was hamstrung by a "problem on both bikes", which meant he was three tenths slower than he had been in Q1. It had a huge knock-on on his grid position and meant his race prospects proved extremely limited as, after barging past Aldeguer, he got stuck behind Acosta and couldn't get the front tyre in a good enough state to give the KTM man anything to worry about.

The Aprilia is clearly better than seventh place here, but on Trackhouse's side the reliability could certainly be improved.

items.title: Norris snatches first Madring Spanish GP pole from Antonelli
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
Lando Norris snatched pole position for the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix from Formula 1 points leader Kimi Antonelli by just 0.011s in a breathless finale to qualifying at the Madring.

With Lewis Hamilton on provisional pole for Ferrari (1m32.079s) ahead of the Mercedes drivers after the first Q3 runs, Red Bull's Max Verstappen and the McLarens of Norris and Oscar Piastri waited until the very end of the session to set their final flying laps.

Norris - who was seventh in Q2 then fifth in Q1 - put in a lap of 1m31.824s right at the very end of Q3 as he found a second of laptime between Q2 and Q3.

He said it was "probably one of the best laps I've ever done" after taking his third pole position of 2026.

Verstappen improved as the clock ran out, but lost time in the final sector to qualify third, behind Antonelli, and 0.140s off Norris's pace.

Hamilton lost time in the first sector but still improved, only to qualify fourth and 0.189s off pole.

Charles Leclerc was just 0.006s behind Ferrari team-mate Hamilton as he rounded out the top five.

Mercedes' George Russell slid out of the final corner on his final effort, losing time and finishing sixth. His pace fell away after a table-topping performance in Q1, as he also finished sixth in Q2.

Piastri was off the pace throughout and finished seventh, 0.470s off his polesitting team-mate.

The other Red Bull of Liam Lawson was almost half a second off in eighth.

Alpine's Franco Colapinto rescued his car after it bottomed out at La Monumental in Q2 as he went on to secure ninth on the grid, having been one second off the pace in Q3.

Arvid Lindblad was two tenths further behind as he put his Racing Bulls 10th.

In Q2, Verstappen set the pace (with a 1m32.431s) to go 0.160s clear of Antonelli.

The speed trap-topping Audis were eliminated in Q2, with Nico Hulkenberg 11th and Gabriel Bortoleto another 0.165s off in 12th.

Esteban Ocon was 13th for Haas.

Monza polesitter Pierre Gasly lost a laptime to double yellows in Q2 and was eventually eliminated in 14th. "Compared to [FP3] it's a completely different car, I don’t get it," he said over the radio.

Replays also showed Gasly tapping the walls on the entry to Turn 16.

Racing Bulls's Yuki Tsunoda had a laptime deleted for track limits in Q2 and could not improve sufficiently. He was eliminated in 15th, one place ahead of Williams's Alex Albon - who was 3.101s off the ultimate pace in Q2.

Madrilenian Carlos Sainz was eliminated in 17th in Q1, having lapped just 0.005s slower than Williams team-mate Albon - who missed FP3 with suspension damage.

Both Aston Martins were eliminated in Q1: Fernando Alonso (18th) missed out by 0.076s and Lance Stroll did not execute a flying lap due to a suspected water pressure issue.

Stroll is set to start at the back of the grid with engine penalties.

The Cadillacs were split by two seconds with Sergio Perez 19th and Valtteri Bottas 20th.

Ollie Bearman failed to turn a lap in Q1 due to his FP3 crash, calling that a "shame" given the potential of his Haas.

items.title: What it's like watching an F1 crash unfolding in front of you
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
It's the crunch that stands out.

That loud, violent, smack of carbonfibre and metal making violent contact with an immovable solid surface is what sticks in your mind when a Formula 1 car crashes into the barriers right in front of you.

It is what stands out recalling those moments at the end of the Spanish Grand Prix's FP3 when Ollie Bearman got it all wrong at the Madring's Turn 10 and ended up smashing into the barriers centimetres in front of me.

It is what I remember from the other time it happened to me, at the Monaco swimming pool back in 2001, when Ralf Schumacher shunted right at the end of opening practice on Thursday.

There is something strange in how your brain processes those moments when the car you are watching is suddenly not doing what you expect it to, and is well off line and travelling in the wrong direction.

You see it is going to go all wrong. You see the tyre smoke. You prepare yourself for the impact. Then the contact happens.

And then, what must be milliseconds later but seems an eternity: that crunch as the sound catches up with the light. It is that which rams home that this is a big one.

After that, the violence dies down, the strewn debris all rolls to a stop, and there is almost a calmness before the marshals get to action.

For a driver, these moments must be even harder to process and the emotions more extreme - as afterwards they appear to go through the classic five stages of grief.

Observing Bearman, as he sits in the Haas making clear to marshals he is OK, you can sense from the way he holds his head and hands the denial and then anger he has about having binned it right at the end of the final practice session.

As he climbs out through a hole in the barriers, there is the depression and then the acceptance of what has happened, as a moped arrives to whisk him away. But he stands there instead, staring into the distance, desperate to watch a crash replay on the big screen behind us.

Then, as the adrenaline winds down, Bearman - since ruled out of qualifying - is beckoned to the medical car. He climbs in the back, looking at the badly damaged Haas still wedged up against the wall. There is the acceptance that it is unlikely that this will not hamper the rest of his weekend.

As Bearman is driven away, the marshals move into action, lifting the car onto a truck and throwing chunks of wrecked carbonfibre through the gaps in the fence.

Drivers had talked before the weekend about the Madring being a punishing venue, and Bearman himself said that the plenty of crashes he had in the sim meant hopefully he had got them out of his system.

"Like that, you learn exactly where the limits are and you find them in the most efficient way possible," he said. "By doing that, you don't do that on the real track, hopefully…"

Unfortunately, real life bites sometimes. And it can be very noisy.

items.title: Marquez outfoxes Bezzecchi to take crucial Misano sprint win
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Defending MotoGP champion Marc Marquez defeated title rival Marco Bezzecchi to win the sprint race at Misano.

Equipped with the medium rear tyre - versus the conventional sprint choice of soft - Marquez pounced on Bezzecchi immediately at the start, using a marginally better getaway to take control of the inside line into Turn 1.

He had far too much pace early on for Bezzecchi, building a lead of over a second - though Bezzecchi did whittle this down to around the 0.5-0.6s mark in the second half of the 13-lap race.But the fastest lap of the race from Marquez on lap 11 broke his resistance, and he settled into second behind Marquez.

Points leader Jorge Martin mitigated the damage by completing the podium - which means he now heads Marquez by 14 points and Bezzecchi by 22.

Fifth after the start, Martin quickly picked off Fermin Aldeguer and then later in the race overtook outside title contender Fabio Di Giannantonio - pouncing at Turn 6 and then fighting off the Ducati on the straight out of the corner.

Di Giannantonio and Alex Marquez completed the top five, the latter having made the most of an Aldeguer v. Pedro Acosta battle up ahead of him to clear both.That battle ended up putting Aldeguer in the firing line of Raul Fernandez, too, and he ultimately came home behind both Acosta and Fernandez, and ahead of last points-scorer Luca Marini.

Fabio Quartararo was the only rider to crash, falling off when he ran out of room trying to squeeze past Diogo Moreira on the inside. He remounted to finish 21st and last.

items.title: Hamilton, Bearman crash in final Madrid F1 practice
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli headed a final Spanish Grand Prix practice session at the Madring featuring two red flags, including one for a Lewis Hamilton crash at the final corner.

Antonelli ended up 0.166s clear of Hamilton's Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc, the long-time pacesetter before the first red flag and after the session resumed, with the McLarens of Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris improving to third and fourth in that period too.

But Hamilton's crash was the session's most noteworthy moment - even if Ollie Bearman's late red-flag inducing crash was the biggest of the Madring weekend yet.

Hamilton had just set the fastest middle sector of all (which still stood as the fastest at the end of the session) when he crashed at the final corner 23 minutes into FP3, locking up and heading nose-first, square-on into the Tecpro barrier.

He found reverse gear from there and, despite protestations from Ferrari to stop the car, attempted to limp his SF-26 back to the pits.

With the front wing rubbing against the front-right tyre, which became punctured, Hamilton did eventually park the Ferrari at Turn 14 - though only after he was told by race engineer Carlo Santi: "It's a formal request, they [the FIA] told us to stop in the safest place possible. Stop before Turn 12 [La Monumental], on the left."

Repairs to the barrier took a significant amount of time, which prompted race control to take the unusual step of pausing the clock to prevent the session time from elapsing before track activity could continue on what is only the second day of official F1 running at the track.

FP3 did finally resume 39 minutes after the red flag was shown with a quarter of an hour left on the clock, a period in which Leclerc improved his best time before Antonelli set the fastest lap of the weekend so far, a 1m32.797s.

Any further changes to the head of the order were prevented by Bearman's crash, which came at Turn 10, the first part of a right-left leading into the circuit's banked La Monumental corner.

Bearman did not appear to clip the wall but lost the car at the apex and spun, which pitched his car backwards into the barrier on the outside of the subsequent left-hand bend.

He was assured by his Haas team afterwards not to worry and that the team would "get it rebuilt" before qualifying, but significant damage to the left-hand side of his car suggested that is far from guaranteed.

Max Verstappen completed just seven laps in the session but ended up fifth-fastest in the best of the Red Bulls, two places but more than seven tenths faster than team-mate Liam Lawson. George Russell was sandwiched between them in the second of the Mercedes cars.

Hamilton's time was still good enough for ninth, with the Audis of Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto either side of him.

Alex Albon was the only driver not to set a time. He glanced the barrier with the left-hand side of his car exiting the penultimate corner and could not rejoin the session, even after the long pause in proceedings.

items.title: How F1 2026 team-mates are comparing in qualifying
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
The 2026 Formula 1 season will allow each driver to compare themselves to their team-mate in full qualifying trim up to 30 times - 24 in grand prix qualifying, and six more in sprint qualifying.

Here's how this year's team-mate pairings are stacking up over one lap so far.

items.title: New Misano lap record from Bezzecchi as he beats Marquez to pole
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
MotoGP title hopeful Marco Bezzecchi dominated qualifying for the San Marino Grand Prix at Misano, seeing off his main rival this weekend Marc Marquez.

A first-ever 1m29s MotoGP lap of Misano - replacing Pecco Bagnaia's 2024 time as the new record, and set in the wheeltracks of Aprilia team-mate and points leader Jorge Martin - propelled Bezzecchi to a huge lead early on in Q2, and meant he didn't have to risk on the second run.

Though the gap was whittled down by the end, nobody got close to Bezzecchi's 1m29.982s.

Marquez bounced back from a mistake early on his second run to deliver the second-fastest lap of the session, two tenths down on Bezzecchi, with Fermin Aldeguer a surprise third for Gresini Ducati.

Aldeguer worked his way through Q1 on his year-old Ducati and found another two tenths between sessions to score his second front row of the year.

Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati) crashed late on but still took fourth, ahead of Martin - whose last-lap attempt went awry at Tramonto - and Honda standout Luca Marini.

Pedro Acosta again led the KTM contingent in seventh, ahead of Di Giannantonio's team-mate Franco Morbidelli, who will serve a long-lap penalty on Sunday for having impeded Enea Bastianini on Friday.

Two Q2 crashes meant a frustrated Alex Marquez could do no better than ninth, but he still outpaced Raul Fernandez (who would have been fifth had he matched his Q1 time), Johann Zarco and Pol Espargaro.

Fabio Quartararo led the Yamaha contingent by six tenths but just didn't have the sectors three-and-four performance to challenge for the top two in Q1, ending up a quarter of a second back in 13th.

He was followed in the order by Bagnaia, who never looked like a big threat for Q2 - even before he scuffed up four successive laps on his second run in Q1.

items.title: F1's TV visuals are letting its Madrid track down
items.author: Edd Straw
items.content:
Television doesn't do the Madring justice.

It's a spectacular place to watch Formula 1 cars, which was clear from heading trackside during FP1 and visiting various vantage points in the first half of the lap during the session. Yet following FP2 from the media centre with sight of the world feed it looked like an entirely different - blander - venue.

Partly, that is the curse of such 'urban' circuits. The nature of such facilities means endless fences, barriers punctuated only by occasional bridges branded by Pirelli, American Express et al, which dominate what fans at home see. It also leaves little room to manoeuvre when it comes to camera positions in terms of space, especially given the need to ensure they offer clean backdrops that aren't polluted by some of the necessary temporary infrastructure such as Portaloos.

This makes it difficult to showcase a circuit that, while certainly no Suzuka or Spa, is a very worthy addition to the calendar. "A commitment track" is how Charles Leclerc characterised it, and that's exactly what drivers and fans desire from the driving challenge of a new circuit. Yet the onboard cameras, which usually sanitise and stabilise the experience, are forced to do the heavy lifting.

It's a privileged position to be able to get up close to the cars when they are running - and this isn’t about arguing viewers should appreciate what they can't see. But while the coverage is, for all the criticisms, excellent (check out a broadcast from 30 years ago to see how far it has come), it's the alpha and omega when it comes to showcasing F1. You cannot build excitement and enthusiasm for a first grand prix, then show it off so poorly.

There's an unavoidable flattening effect from filming that is impossible to get around, and no matter how many races you see from Spa before you visit, your reaction to seeing the steep incline of Eau Rouge in person will always take your breath away.

This means the elevation change at Madring will be subdued on screen. But what doesn't come over so well is just how unforgiving it is, giving drivers little or no margin for error in many places where there can be big laptime gains, or losses, in committing that little bit more. This side of Madring should be experienced by everyone, not just those on the ground.

The banked corner of La Monumental is a great example. Conceived as a Mexico stadium-style cauldron, where spectators crowd the corner, it is a uniquely long turn with big consequences should things go wrong - yet it becomes flat on TV. The low angle and the not-quite-high-enough elevated angle diminish its grandeur. And parts of the track resemble just another Miami/Sochi-style venue.

Part of that is the surroundings. It's built in and around the IFEMA exhibition centre, which by definition will comprise large halls and their infrastructure. In some ways, this is used well with the distinctive indoor team trucks/engineering hubs (as opposed to the hospitality units, which are outside). But it poses limitations because the environs are, fundamentally, bland. There's little that screams 'Madrid' about it, partly because it's outlying rather than in the city centre.

It will improve next year, even if no conscious action is taken - because the Madring will have had time to bed in, it will be tidier and cleaner. Camera locations and views will be optimised and that should at least close the gap.

None of this is easy and plenty of effort will have already gone into showing it off well, but there must also be some serious thinking in how to present a charismatic circuit that genuinely adds something unique to the calendar more faithfully.

The design of the ribbon of asphalt is the key part of any F1 newcomer, and Madring has done a good job with that, but more can be done to show that to the outside world.

items.title: F1 teams face big Madring strategy dilemma
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Formula 1 isn't really heading for the six-stopper Spanish Grand Prix that George Russell half joked was on the cards after opening practice.

But tyre supplier Pirelli says a combination of factors at F1's newest venue means strategy is going to be particularly tricky to work out.

In fact, the initial prediction following Friday's running is that teams are going to be stuck between a rock and a hard place when working out what is best to do.

The super-long pitlane, which has left the pitstop loss time at around 24 seconds, is a deterrent for tyre changes and means the most logical route should be a one-stopper.

But high levels of thermal degradation of the rubber, and particularly challenging front left graining, means that a two-stop would be sensible.

With no middle ground between those two choices, it is not going to be a case of what is the best strategy to pick. It is about which is the least bad.

F1 teams were left wide-eyed after opening practice when the tyre degradation looked pretty extreme.

A combination of high grip asphalt (highest of the season according to Pirelli), a smooth surface and fast corners has meant cars are sliding a lot – and that triggered some alarming findings during that first session.

As Russell said: "It's often a possibility on new tarmacs that the grip is very high but you're sliding quite aggressively.

"With the deg we had in FP1, a six-stop race would have been the fastest way. FP2 was slightly better and I'm sure the race on Sunday will be better again. But that's the biggest question mark."  

From Pirelli's perspective, there are two issues that drivers and teams are going to have to manage as the Spanish GP weekend continues – and neither is particularly straightforward.

The most complex issue is front left graining, which is being generated because the combination of the smooth surface and high grip means the rubber hits peak stress easily and the surface effectively tears.

Front graining triggers mid-corner understeer and a subsequent drop in performance. It is much harder to manage on the kind of high-speed corners that feature at the Madring than it is at low-speed venues.

Oscar Piastri said after Friday that this element had been the biggest headache from running.

"It's been a nightmare to try and manage the tyres with graining," he said. "It normally gets better through a weekend, but we'll have to wait and see how much better."

It is not just the fronts that are proving to be hard to deal with around the Madring, because the high-speed corners and the way the cars are almost constantly in turns means that the rears are overheating too.

Throw these two elements together and the result is high degradation.

Pirelli chief engineer Simone Berra reckoned that the drop off here was at a "very high" level – around 0.2-0.3 seconds per lap based on some of the long runs in FP2.

"It was a surprise to have these kinds of values," he said. "They were outside our range of expectations."

While general track evolution and improved set-ups should help reduce that figure by the time the race comes around, the scene is set for the Spanish GP turning into a race where tyre strategy will be critical.

That is what has fuelled all teams apart from Audi electing to keep two hard tyres back after Friday practice – as that could well be the most resilient option for Sunday.

Berra said that the unpredictability thrown up by the front graining and overheating, plus the levels of the degradation, meant that plotting the right path through the race was going to be tough to nail.

"I don't want to exclude any kind of situation," he said. "I think looking from the data, you would think that the teams will go for a two-stop because the degradation is very high.

"But the pitstop loss is 24 seconds, so I'm pretty sure that some teams will try to reach as a target the one-stop race.

"It means we could end up in different situations, with some teams trying the one-stop and other teams trying the two-stops."

Which route is best is unclear right now, and matters are further complicated by how difficult it could be to overtake.

For even though the new power units mean deployment offsets can make passes easier at some venues than in the past, equally there are downsides to falling into the pack.

Berra added: "If you are in traffic, you lose quite a lot of performance, and you also destroy your tyres because you lose load and you generate high temperatures as you're sliding.

"So, we have different factors that are pushing teams towards different directions. 

"It's not easy; in fact, it is pretty complicated."

items.title: The surprise plan to keep Alonso in F1
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem is working on a fresh rules concession plan to help accelerate Honda’s progress and keep Fernando Alonso in Formula 1.

Alonso is currently weighing up whether he wants to stay in grand prix racing next year, as he feels little excitement for F1’s current regulations and is facing competitive uncertainties too.

It has emerged at the Spanish Grand Prix, however, that efforts are underway behind the scenes to give Aston Martin’s struggling engine supplier Honda an extra helping hand for 2027 – and therefore boost Alonso’s incentive to remain.

Fresh from a difficult Italian Grand Prix outing for Honda’s upgraded power unit, Ben Sulayem met with Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll on Thursday to discuss a potential action plan that can help both his squad’s competitive fortunes and secure a fresh contract with Alonso.

It is understood that the FIA president, having spoken to Alonso at Monza, plans further talks with the two-time world champion in Madrid to try push forward with a package of measures that can help.

Earlier this year, the FIA helped secure agreement from all manufacturers for Honda to be granted extra assistance under the ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) catch-up mechanism.

This opened the door for Honda to get more test bench hours plus the ability to secure an extra $19 million spending package – although some of this was taken as a theoretical loan against its own future development budget.

It is unclear what fresh assistance Stroll and Alonso are chasing now, and sources suggest that discussions have not yet got as far as any formal rule change details being focused on and talked about in detail with Honda.

Options could involve more homologation freedoms, extra spending allowances or even specific rule changes in areas where Honda feels that its progress is being limited. 

Any tweaks to the rules would need support from other manufacturers, however, who showed earlier this year that they were willing to put self-interest aside to assist.

Sources have told The Race that Ben Sulayem is determined to do everything in his power to help push this matter through, as he thinks this would be of benefit to F1 as a whole.

That is because he wants to avoid a situation where Honda is stuck where it is – which would risk both Alonso walking and the Japanese engine manufacturer itself even pondering its own future in F1 if it continues to face difficulties on track.

Speaking at the New Economy Forum event in Madrid on Friday morning, Ben Sulayem spoke about how a chat he had with Alonso at the Italian GP had sparked a call to action.

He revealed that he was awaiting some feedback from Alonso about what the FIA can do to assist things.

“I saw him very sad,” said Ben Sulayem. “I said, Fernando, I understand that it's not acceptable that you are coming to your own country, and then now, after two times [being] the world champion, you are in the last [place]. 

“We did something earlier in May, legally, for the team, towards the engine, to go and improve.

“I said to him, I'm not going to tell you what we are going to do. Please tell me what you want! Because you are the driver, come and tell me what do you want us to do, to improve these results.”

On Thursday, Alonso hinted at potential changes being on the horizon beyond the fuel flow increase that has been set in stone.

His comments caused intrigue in the paddock, but now appear to be related to his conversations with Ben Sulayem.

“I still have some hope that next year’s rule will still have to be tweaked again, that this is not the final version,” he said.

Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack said at the Madring circuit that a decision on Alonso’s future would depend on a lot of factors. But he had faith that, whatever it was Alonso wanted, it would be seen through.

I think he made clear that it is not one single thing that he wants to see change,” explained Krack. “I think the sport needs someone like that. I think we will all be keen to see Fernando continue.

“And what can be done to accommodate, I think it will be done. And then I hope we come to a good solution and continue.” 

Ben Sulayem is emphatic that he will do what he can to ensure that this is not Alonso’s final year in F1.

“There's no way we can allow Fernando to leave,” he said. “He has to be successful, and then he leaves whenever he wants, not because he was forced to leave because of the performance.”

items.title: Winners and losers from F1 Madring practice
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
The first day of proper Formula 1 on-track running at the Madring didn't produce the predicted chaos.

But it did provide some early winners and losers...

A first day of F1 track action at a venue is always scary times, especially for a track that was tipped to be an immediate cauldron of chaos.

This was largely true in Formula 3 and Formula 2 - but the Formula 1 grid by and large kept things tidy, and first impressions up and down the field seem seriously positive.

This has to be caveated with the note that, as always, it's in everyone's best interest to speak highly of the new race, and there are serious question marks over the quality of race action on Sunday - though unexpectedly high tyre wear might help.

But the track is getting early approval.

"We've seen street circuits come and go in Formula 1 - and it feels already like this is one that's here to stay," rejoiced Mercedes deputy team boss Bradley Lord.

"I think putting the perfect lap together tomorrow in qualifying is going to be a real challenge and that's exactly what it should be."

"I think it's a very, very impressive facility," said Racing Bulls chief Alan Permane. "It doesn't feel like a new street track they've just sort of slapped down in a car park, it really feels like they've taken some time and effort and put together a really interesting circuit. Really impressed."

Drivers weren't necessarily unanimous (Max Verstappen, for instance, just doesn't care for street circuits in principle, as he admitted), but there was significant praise on that end, too, with Pierre Gasly saying he "really loved it" and Charles Leclerc appreciating a "commitment" track with higher grip than expected.

OK, not everybody kept it clean - with Lindblad the outlier, triggering a long slide that ended with a right-rear-first smack into the Turn 13 barriers.

"It looked quite bad, but actually the impact was not very hard," he said afterwards. "Charles did it in much more spectacular fashion in Monza! 

"Yeah, there's a bit of damage, it's a good amount, quite a lot, but nothing that's not repairable. So I just apologise to the engineers, but especially the mechanics, because they've got a bit of extra work tonight, unfortunately." -

Winner: Arvid Lindblad, also

Even with the crash, both Lindblad and his boss Permane were remarkably, tellingly bullish - believing his mere 0.228s deficit to the front was a genuine signal.

"It's not really mixed emotions, I'd much rather be in 4th place with a damaged car than 18th place with a car with four wheels on," enthused Permane. 

"It's not ideal of course, and we certainly can't do that every weekend - but we can accept that. 

"There's no doubt the car is quick, very quick, it's properly P4 pace today, and I don't say it'll be P4 pace tomorrow afternoon, but it'll be right up there, I think."

Lindblad said: "We were P4 on merit. Every lap we did in FP2 we were fast, so that's the most important thing."

Golden rule at a new F1 track: get as many laps in during practice to make sure you're prepared.

Sadly, McLaren couldn't follow that rule as a gearbox failure ruled Lando Norris out of any meaningful running in FP2. A big opportunity to get the car and driver in the right window.

If that wasn't bad enough, Oscar Piastri, who did get the two practices in, said that the team is "lacking pace".

We've seen McLaren turn things around from difficult Fridays before, but the usual Mercedes juggernaut and what looks like a resurgent Ferrari certainly make this look like a tough event ahead.

The upgrade Haas debuted on both cars at Monza was always expected to work better at the Madring and the early on-track evidence supports that. 

Esteban Ocon was ninth in FP2, calling it a “very good day” after practice, with early indications suggesting he doesn’t have the car inconsistency issues that limited him at Monza.

“There doesn't seem to be the inconsistency that we had in Monza,” Ocon said.

“We've changed many parts on the car again, and now it seems to be working quite well.

“We need to have a deep dive tonight to see what has improved exactly, but so far, driving the car, I'm not feeling that today there was an issue. 

“We need to obviously keep that going for tomorrow. Overall, it's been pretty good.” 

He also suggested the prevalence of tyre graining at this circuit is good news for Haas, which suffers less from it than its rivals do.

The best part of Red Bull's day was Verstappen's retort when asked if he would have wanted more given where Lindblad (fourth in FP2) was, and Max's hilarious reply was "I don't drive that car, so I don't know how fast it is".

Verstappen merely pointed to needing to improve the balance, while team-mate Liam Lawson complained of a lack of rear grip. Still, it was a complicated day, as even though Verstappen finished higher up the order in FP1, in fourth, he was closer to the Mercedes' pace in FP2 when he was sixth.

It's fair to say we haven't got a clear picture of where the Red Bull/McLaren/Ferrari picture lies, but Ferrari certainly seems to have the upper hand at the moment, and Red Bull might be F1's fourth-best team, again.

Such a tough track still has the potential to catch 2026’s benchmark team out, but for now Mercedes looks reasonably comfortable out front with George Russell and Kimi Antonelli topping a practice session each. 

“We started well in FP1, and the car was strong from the off,” FP1 pacesetter Russell said. 

“We made some set-up changes for FP2, but I’m not sure they improved the car, so we may row back on them overnight.” 

From the limited long-run data, there’s nothing to suggest Mercedes doesn’t head into the rest of the weekend as the marginal favourites once again.
